extracted.intended_audience: literate London readers, theatre-goers, and people interested in manners, conversation, courtship, and theatrical criticism (early-18th-century readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive essays on qualities of a 'man of conversation' and practical norms for courtship, acting, and playwriting — i.e., how to behave well in society and how to evaluate theatrical performance and dramatic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gentleman / man of conversation — essential qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally thought, that warmth of imagination, quick relish of pleasure, and a manner of becoming it, are the most essential qualities for forming this sort of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrounding explanation: though imagination and relish of pleasure matter, the supreme mark of good breeding is shown in never giving offence. A true man of conversation has a good judgment, masters his companion without letting him see it, acts with ease among both pleasure and business people, is neither nor appears cunning, performs good offices with readiness and alacrity, and denies what he will not engage in in a manner that convinces you you ought not to have asked it. His conversation should be a 'continual feast' that maintains equality of society and keeps him desired by women without envying men.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good judgment as the central conversational talent
rubrics_metrics.description: The most necessary talent therefore in a man of conversation ... is a good judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: good judgment allows a man to be master of his company without showing it, to adapt to varied companions, to act discreetly (so as not to appear cunning), to contribute cheerfully, and to keep society equal. This is presented as the defining quality above wit or mere entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good breeding = never giving offence
rubrics_metrics.description: The height of good breeding is shown rather in never giving offence, than in doing obliging things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/anti-patterns: A person who never shocks you, though seldom entertaining, will keep favour more than one who sometimes entertains but sometimes displeases. Thus restraint and avoidance of offence are prioritized over showy politeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pretty Fellow (inauthentic mimicry) — what to avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: The Pretty Fellow imitates natural behaviour artificially: being just able to find out that what makes Sophronius acceptable is a natural behaviour, in order to the same reputation, makes his own an artificial one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples/anti-patterns: Jack Dimple (the 'Pretty Fellow') is a perfect mimic who uses mirrors, affects airs, meditates on his appearance and returns to the glass — an artificial performance of sociability. This is presented as a fault: affectation rather than genuine disposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting should be natural and avoid overacting
rubrics_metrics.description: There is certainly nature excellently represented in his manner of action; in which he ever avoided that general fault in players, of doing too much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cave Underhill is praised for natural comedy and for avoiding 'doing too much.' Anti-pattern: actors who overact or who 'do too much' are faulted. Further note: actors who have gone out of the world without ever speaking any original words are not to be praised for adding to the author's text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actors should not be allowed to grow rich on the profession
rubrics_metrics.description: They will not allow anybody to grow rich on a profession that in their opinion so little conduces to the good of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context/example: In Amsterdam actors are tradesmen who perform after their day's work and theatre profits maintain a hospital. The social norm emphasised: acting is not treated as a sole, wealth-accumulating vocation; proceeds are used for public benefit (e.g., hospital).

rubrics_metrics.name: Playwriting / character-differentiation: speech should fit and distinguish characters
rubrics_metrics.description: No one sentence in a play should be spoken by any one character, which could possibly enter into the head of any other man represented in it; but every sentiment should be peculiar to him only who utters it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and caveats: The essay argues for distinctiveness of voice and sentiment among characters so that each appears singular; Ben Jonson's works are cited as able to bear such scrutiny, while some modern writers rely on costume rather than dialect to distinguish characters. The piece warns that if modern writers were scrutinised this way, many plays would be too short — indicating a tension between distinctive speech and theatrical length/entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern playwriting: use habit/attire to indicate role versus dialect differentiation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is no difficulty to get hats, and swords, and wigs, and shoes, and everything else, from the shops in town, and make a man show himself by his habit, without more ado, to be a counsellor, a fop, a courtier, or a citizen, and not be obliged to make those characters talk in different dialects to be distinguished from each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance/critique: This is presented as 'the surest and best way of writing' for contemporary convenience, but it is critiqued because it can encourage homogenous speech across characters and rob the audience of pleasure when a play's lines don't match character background. The passage highlights tradeoffs between visual shorthand and literary distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courtship / 'ogling' skill: exquisite judgment of glances
rubrics_metrics.description: Ogling with skill carries a woman ... This requires an exquisite judgment, to take the language of her eyes to yours exactly, and not let yours talk too fast for hers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance and example: repeated, well-timed looks (four or five significant looks) build a lover's imagination, causing him to idealise external objects and past images; mis-timed or hurried glances are counterproductive. The passage presents skilled mutual eye-language as an art to be cultivated, not an accidental behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical/social diagnosis: prefer natural explanations to supernatural ones
rubrics_metrics.description: The parson ... supposes ... ordinary causes (drunkenness, butcher's daughter carrying meat, gingerbread stamped with images) rather than witchcraft to explain alleged phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: when encountering sensational accusations (witchcraft, sorcery), prefer mundane and testable explanations; the parson's approach is presented approvingly as a rational antidote to popular superstition.
